## Abstract

This study investigates the ecological impacts of land use change, particularly focusing on the vegetation near the Temae Golf Course on Moorea, French Polynesia. Through field surveys conducted by the 2024 Island Sustainability Program cohort, we compare plant diversity and composition in pristine and cultivated areas adjacent to the golf course. Our findings highlight significant differences, with cultivated areas exhibiting lower diversity and a higher proportion of introduced species. These results underscore the potential risks associated with tourism-driven land development, including the introduction of invasive species and the loss of ecosystem resilience. By shedding light on these impacts, our study emphasizes the importance of integrating conservation efforts with tourism development to ensure the long-term sustainability of Moorea’s ecosystems.

## Abstract

The atrocities of imperial nuclear testing in the Pacific Ocean have gone without widespread recognition or addressing for too long. Health effects caused by radiation exposure can be screened for and examined genetically. The objective of this project is to collect data regarding the genetic health of ethnic Pacific Islanders on the island of Mo’orea; this data will be used to properly assess the lasting genetic and genomic effects of nuclear testing on Pacific Islanders, and to facilitate genetic counseling to individuals at no cost.

## Abstract

Standard bulk probes of multiband superconductors cannot assign pairing gaps to specific electron or hole Fermi surfaces. Here we show that thermal Hall transport ( $\kappa_{xy}$ ), constrained by specific heat and normal-state magnetotransport, resolves this ambiguity in the compensated heavy-fermion superconductor CeRu2. Fixing the gap magnitudes via specific heat ( $\Delta_{e}/k_{\mathrm{B}}\approx$13\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$$ , $\Delta_{h}/k_{\mathrm{B}}\approx$8\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$$ ), and band mobilities completely determines the normal-state electronic degrees of freedom. A low-field sign reversal in $\kappa_{xy}$ places the larger gap on the heavy Ce $4f$ electron sheets and the smaller on the hole sheets.

Many superconductors host multiple Fermi-surface sheets across which the pairing gap can vary substantially [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. This phenomenon is particularly significant in heavy-fermion superconductors, where Kondo hybridization delocalizes $f$ -electrons into heavy Fermi-surface sheets that coexist with lighter conduction bands, obscuring how quasiparticle mass renormalization governs participation in the superconducting condensate [7, 8, 9, 10, 11]. Establishing how gap magnitudes are distributed among distinct bands is essential for linking a material’s electronic structure to its pairing mechanism [12, 13, 14]. However, standard bulk thermodynamic probes—such as specific heat, penetration depth, and longitudinal thermal conductivity $\kappa_{xx}$ —measure a sum over all sheets weighted by their respective densities of states or velocities [15, 16, 17, 18]. Because these probes are insensitive to carrier sign, they struggle to determine which Fermi-surface sheet hosts which gap, nor can they unambiguously distinguish multiband pairing from gap anisotropy on a single sheet [19, 20, 21].

A bulk probe sensitive to carrier sign can directly overcome this limitation. Whereas the electrical Hall conductivity vanishes in the superconducting state, the thermal Hall conductivity $\kappa_{xy}$ remains finite in the mixed state and selectively tracks the entropy transport of thermally excited Bogoliubov quasiparticles (BQPs) without a competing phonon background [22, 23]. Although the exponential freeze-out of BQPs below $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ is governed by each band’s respective gap scale [24, 25], gaps of comparable magnitude suppress these excitations across overlapping temperature windows. Developing a robust $\kappa_{xy}$ methodology to disentangle multiple superconducting gaps and assign them to specific Fermi surface sheets is therefore essential for resolving the underlying pairing mechanisms in correlated and flat-band superconductors.

The cubic Laves-phase superconductor CeRu2 ( $T_{\mathrm{c}}\approx$6\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$$ ) provides an ideal platform for this test. Band-structure calculations and de Haas–van Alphen measurements establish a compensated metal with electron- and hole-like Fermi-surface sheets of equal total volume [26]. Carrier compensation renders the thermal Hall response exceptionally sensitive to modest differences between gaps: because the oppositely signed electron and hole contributions nearly cancel in the normal state, the net sign of $\kappa_{xy}$ is governed by a slight mobility imbalance. Below $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ , the band with the larger gap freezes out more rapidly; if that band dominates the normal-state Hall response, even a moderate gap hierarchy will trigger a complete sign reversal of $\kappa_{xy}$ upon cooling. In CeRu2, photoemission, muon spin-rotation ( $\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro}$ ) spectroscopy, and thermodynamic studies have long pointed to a nonuniform gap structure [27, 28, 29, 30], yet whether this reflects single-band anisotropy or distinct gaps on separate sheets has remained unresolved for over two decades. Crucially, because both Ru $4d$ and hybridized itinerant Ce $4f$ states contribute at the Fermi level [31]—with the electron sheets near $\Gamma$ carrying predominantly $4f$ character and the heaviest effective masses—identifying which carrier type hosts the dominant gap directly illuminates the role of $4f$ electrons in the pairing state.

*Figure 1: Compensated two-band transport and two-gap superconducting state in CeRu2. (a) Specific heat $C/T$ in the normal state (squares, teal curve) and superconducting state (circles, red curve), showing fits to a single-gap (gray dashed curve) and two-gap (red curve) BCS model. The inset highlights the low-temperature deviation of the single-gap fit ( $\Delta/k_{\mathrm{B}}=$12.1\pm\pm 0.1\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$$ ). (b) Electron and hole mobilities ( $\mu_{e}$ and $\mu_{h}$ ) and their ratio extracted from a compensated two-band magnetotransport model, yielding $\mu_{h}/\mu_{e}=0.68$ (dashed line). (c) Longitudinal ( $L_{xx}$ ) and transverse ( $L_{xy}$ ) Lorenz ratios at $9\text{\,}\mathrm{T}$ normalized by the Sommerfeld value $L_{0}$ . The dashed line marks the Wiedemann–Franz expectation ( $L/L_{0}=1$ ). (d) Zero-field $\kappa_{xx}/T$ below $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ , showing the strong enhancement of the phonon thermal conductivity ( $\kappa_{\mathrm{ph}}$ , green) as the electron-band ( $\kappa_{xx,e}$ , blue) and hole-band ( $\kappa_{xx,h}$ , red) quasiparticle channels are gapped out. The solid black curve is the total thermal conductivity from the combined two-gap BRT and Debye–Callaway model.*

Here we demonstrate that combining thermal Hall transport with zero-field thermodynamics and magnetotransport uniquely assigns superconducting gaps of comparable magnitude to their respective Fermi-surface sheets. In CeRu2, zero-field specific heat fixes two distinct temperature-equivalent gap scales ( $8\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$ and $13\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$ , respectively) while the normal-state mobility ratio $\mu_{h}/\mu_{e}$ locks in their relative transport weights, completely constraining the two-band Bardeen–Rickayzen–Tewordt (BRT) electronic channels in $\kappa_{xx}$ against a pronounced phonon enhancement. Extending this parameter-independent BRT decomposition to $\kappa_{xy}$ via band-dependent thermal Hall angles, we show that a prominent low-field sign reversal of $\kappa_{xy}$ upon cooling from an electron-dominated normal state unambiguously places the larger gap on the heavy, Ce $4f$ -derived electron sheets and the smaller gap on the hole sheets, before giving way at higher fields to a quadratic mixed-state recovery up to the upper critical field $H_{\mathrm{c}2}$ .

We begin by characterizing the bulk superconducting state of CeRu2 single crystals [see Supplemental Material (SM) for experimental methods]. Figure 1(a) displays the specific heat in both the superconducting (circles, $\mu_{0}H=$0\text{\,}\mathrm{T}$$ ) and normal (squares, $\mu_{0}H=$7\text{\,}\mathrm{T}$$ ) states. A fit to the normal-state data yields a Sommerfeld coefficient $\gamma_{n}=$28.1\pm\pm 0.3\text{\,}\mathrm{mJ}\text{\,}{\mathrm{mol}}^{-1}\text{\,}{\mathrm{K}}^{-2}$$ [32, 33], reflecting a moderately enhanced electronic density of states. Subtracting the lattice contribution from the $0\text{\,}\mathrm{T}$ data (teal curve, see SM for more details) isolates the electronic specific heat, which exhibits clear low-temperature deviations from an isotropic single-gap BCS description [Fig. 1(a) and inset, gray dashed curve]. Instead, a two-gap BCS model [25] accurately captures the data across the full temperature range [Fig. 1(a), red curve], yielding a dominant gap $\Delta_{e}/k_{\mathrm{B}}=$13.0\pm\pm 0.1\text{\,}\mathrm{K}${}$ and a smaller gap $\Delta_{h}/k_{\mathrm{B}}=$8.1\pm\pm 0.2\text{\,}\mathrm{K}${}$ (whose respective electron and hole assignments are established by $\kappa_{xy}$ below). While $\Delta_{e}$ lies near the upper bound of previously reported gap scales in CeRu2 ( $8.1$ – $12.8\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$ and $2.3$ – $5.8\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$ ), $\Delta_{h}$ exceeds earlier estimates [30, 28, 27, 29]. This difference arises because prior studies typically characterized the order parameter using an anisotropic single-band model, and because the modest gap ratio ( $\Delta_{e}/\Delta_{h}\approx 1.6$ ) produces subtle thermodynamic inflection points that are easily obscured without high-resolution low-temperature data.

To constrain how these two gaps partition the electronic heat current, we extract the normal-state carrier parameters via magnetotransport (see SM). Fitting the longitudinal and Hall conductivities to a compensated two-band model ( $n_{e}=n_{h}$ ) yields a total carrier density $n=$3.6\text{\times}{10}^{21}\text{\,}{\mathrm{cm}}^{-3}$$ and a temperature-independent mobility ratio $\mu_{h}/\mu_{e}=0.68$ [Fig. 1(b)]. We next connect the normal-state charge and entropy currents through the Lorenz ratios $L_{ij}=\kappa_{ij}/(\sigma_{ij}T)$ for $ij\in\{xx,xy\}$ . Figure 1(c) compares $L_{xx}$ and $L_{xy}$ at $9\text{\,}\mathrm{T}$ against the Sommerfeld value $L_{0}\approx$2.44\text{\times}{10}^{-8}\text{\,}\mathrm{W}\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolOhm}\text{\,}{\mathrm{K}}^{-2}$$ . On cooling below $10\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$ , $L_{xx}$ approaches $L_{0}$ from above while $L_{xy}$ remains comparable in magnitude with a modest suppression at higher temperatures, confirming a predominantly electronic normal-state heat current. Crucially, the low-temperature recovery of the Wiedemann–Franz law ( $L_{xx}\to L_{0}$ ) determines the total normal-state electronic thermal conductivity $\kappa_{\mathrm{el}}=L_{0}\sigma_{xx}T$ directly from the $9\text{\,}\mathrm{T}$ electrical conductivity, while carrier compensation fixes the relative hole-to-electron normal-state thermal conductance ratio to $\mu_{h}/\mu_{e}=0.68$ .

In zero field, $\kappa_{xx}/T$ exhibits a pronounced enhancement below $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ [Fig. 1(d)], driven by the interplay between the collective phonon and electronic channels. Because the superconducting condensate carries no entropy, electronic heat transport below $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ is mediated exclusively by thermally excited Bogoliubov quasiparticles (BQPs). For an $s$ -wave superconductor, the BQP entropy content and its resulting thermal conductivity are governed by Bardeen–Rickayzen–Tewordt (BRT) theory [24]. Simultaneously, as the opening of the superconducting gaps depletes the BQP population, phonon-electron scattering is strongly suppressed, elongating the phonon mean free path and driving the observed surge in the lattice thermal conductivity $\kappa_{\mathrm{ph}}$ [Fig. 1(d), green curve].

Crucially, our normal-state transport and specific heat measurements completely determine the electronic thermal conductivity below $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ without free parameters. We model the electronic channel as the sum of two independent $s$ -wave BRT contributions corresponding to the electron and hole bands, highlighted by the blue ( $\kappa_{xx,e}$ ) and red ( $\kappa_{xx,h}$ ) curves in Fig. 1(d). The magnitudes and temperature dependencies of the respective gaps are fixed directly by our zero-field specific heat data, while the fractional hole-band weight ( $0.4$ ) is fixed by the normal-state mobility ratio $\mu_{h}/\mu_{e}$ (see SM), reflecting a compensated carrier system with a small, negative normal-state Hall coefficient.

With the electronic channels $\kappa_{xx,e}$ and $\kappa_{xx,h}$ fully constrained ( $\kappa_{\mathrm{el}}=\kappa_{xx,e}+\kappa_{xx,h}$ ), the remaining degrees of freedom reside entirely within the lattice channel $\kappa_{\mathrm{ph}}=\kappa_{xx}-\kappa_{\mathrm{el}}$ . We capture $\kappa_{\mathrm{ph}}$ accurately using a Debye–Callaway model that incorporates the BRT-prescribed reduction in phonon-BQP scattering below $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ [Fig. 1(d), solid black curve; see SM]. Furthermore, attributing the low-temperature thermal conductivity to a two-band BQP channel rather than an unphysically large phonon background is independently corroborated by the rapid recovery of $\kappa_{xx}(H)$ in the mixed state below $0.75H_{\mathrm{c}2}$ , where vortex scattering would otherwise strongly damp lattice transport (see SM). Deconstructing $\kappa_{xx}$ into its band-resolved electronic ( $\kappa_{xx,e},\kappa_{xx,h}$ ) and phononic ( $\kappa_{\mathrm{ph}}$ ) components provides the direct foundation needed to link our longitudinal transport to the thermal Hall conductivity $\kappa_{xy}$ via the thermal Hall angle.

We next examine $\kappa_{xy}$ , which selectively probes electronic excitations and their signed band contributions without a competing phonon background. In the normal state, $\kappa_{xy}/(\mu_{0}HT)=-\lambda_{0}$ is field- and temperature-independent [34], with $\lambda_{0}\approx$1.6\text{\times}{10}^{-3}\text{\,}\mathrm{W}\text{\,}{\mathrm{K}}^{-2}\text{\,}{\mathrm{m}}^{-1}\text{\,}{\mathrm{T}}^{-1}$$ , and the transverse Lorenz ratio remains close to $L_{0}$ [Fig. 1(c)]. This confirms that $\kappa_{xy}$ is governed exclusively by charge carriers; moreover, below $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ , the exponential freeze-out of both signed channels as $T\rightarrow 0$ [Fig. 3(b)]—in stark contrast to the large phonon peak in $\kappa_{\mathrm{ph}}$ [Fig. 1(d)]—rules out any anomalous phonon skew-scattering contribution in the vortex state. Entering the superconducting state at low fields, $\kappa_{xy}$ tracks the thermally excited BQP populations across the two carrier bands, resolving a prominent sign inversion below $1\text{\,}\mathrm{T}$ on cooling [Fig. 2(a)]. With increasing field, this sign reversal is rapidly suppressed and gives way to a quadratic-in-field recovery of $\kappa_{xy}/T$ toward the normal state [Fig. 2(b)], accompanied at $2.1\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$ by a sharp low-field peak below $1\text{\,}\mathrm{T}$ [Fig. 2(b), inset] that mirrors previously measured heavy-fermion superconductors [22, 35].

*Figure 2: Thermal Hall conductivity of CeRu2 in the mixed state. (a) Temperature dependence of $\kappa_{xy}/(\mu_{0}H)$ showing a prominent sign reversal at $0.5\text{\,}\mathrm{T}$ that is rapidly suppressed with increasing field. Lines are guides to the eye. (b) Field dependence of $\kappa_{xy}/T$ , exhibiting a quadratic-in-field recovery toward the normal state. At $2.1\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$ , a low-field peak emerges below $1\text{\,}\mathrm{T}$ (magnified in the inset).*

*Figure 3: Two-band origin of the mixed-state thermal Hall sign reversal and $H$ – $T$ phase diagram of CeRu2. (a) Temperature dependence of $\kappa_{xy}/(\mu_{0}HT)$ in the mixed state at fixed fields, tracking the low-field sign reversal below $1\text{\,}\mathrm{T}$ . Solid curves are two-band fits to Eq. (1). (b) Decomposed electron (blue) and hole (red) contributions to the thermal Hall conductivity at $0.5\text{\,}\mathrm{T}$ . (c) Thermal Hall conductivity normalized by the extrapolated normal-state behavior, $\kappa_{xy}/\kappa_{xy}^{(n)}$ . Solid lines are linear fits to Eq. (2) in the intermediate-field regime. (d) Field dependence of the two-band fitting coefficients $b_{e}$ and $b_{h}$ ; dashed lines are guides to the eye. (e) $H$ – $T$ phase diagram of CeRu2 overlaid on an intensity map of $\kappa_{xy}/\kappa_{xy}^{(n)}$ . Black circles and red triangles mark $H_{\mathrm{c}2}$ and the magnetic irreversibility ( $H^{*}$ ) extracted from magnetization (see SM), respectively. The light gray curve is a Werthamer–Helfand–Hohenberg (WHH) fit to the upper critical field $H_{\mathrm{c}2}$ [36].*

To quantify how the band-resolved longitudinal channels govern this behavior, we link $\kappa_{xy}$ to our zero-field BRT decomposition via the band-dependent thermal Hall angles $\tan\theta_{i}(H)=\kappa_{xy,i}/\kappa_{xx,i}$ :

$$ \frac{\kappa_{xy}}{T}=\lambda_{0}\left[-b_{e}(H)R_{e}(T)+b_{h}(H)R_{h}(T)\right], $$

where $R_{e,h}(T)\leq 1$ are the parameter-free BRT suppression factors fixed by specific heat for the electron and hole gaps. Here, the field-dependent weights $b_{i}(H)=(\kappa_{xx,i}^{(n)}/\lambda_{0}T)\lvert\tan\theta_{i}(H)\rvert$ encapsulate the normal-state band conductivities $\kappa_{xx,i}^{(n)}$ (fixed by $\mu_{h}/\mu_{e}$ ) and their respective Hall angles. The factorization of the field and temperature dependencies in Eq. (1) is well justified in the low-field limit ( $H\ll H_{\mathrm{c}2}$ ). Because our crystals lie in the moderately dirty limit ( $\ell_{i}\leq\xi_{0}$ ; see SM), elastic impurity scattering dominates the normal-state relaxation rate, pinning $\tau_{i}$ below $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ so that the temperature evolution of $\kappa_{xy}/T$ at fixed field is governed by the BQP freeze-out $R_{i}(T)$ . Fitting Eq. (1) over $$2.3\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$<T<$5.8\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$$ under the normal-state boundary condition $b_{e}(H)-b_{h}(H)=\mu_{0}H$ accurately captures the low-field temperature evolution and sign reversal [Fig. 3(a,b)]. Remarkably, the extracted coefficients $b_{e}(H)$ and $b_{h}(H)$ reveal a crossover near $1\text{\,}\mathrm{T}$ from compensated two-carrier transport to an electron-dominated regime [Fig. 3(d)], directly accounting for the low-field peak observed at base temperature in Fig. 2(b).

At intermediate fields ( $$1\text{\,}\mathrm{T}$<\mu_{0}H<\mu_{0}H_{\mathrm{c}2}$ ), the quadratic-in-field recovery of $\kappa_{xy}$ seen in Fig. 2(b) translates to a linear variation of the normalized response $\kappa_{xy}/\kappa_{xy}^{(n)}$ with field [Fig. 3(c)]. Because $\kappa_{xy}^{(n)}=-\lambda_{0}\mu_{0}HT$ is purely linear in $H$ , this intermediate-field regime—reflecting an odd-in-field $H\lvert H\rvert$ contribution alongside a residual linear term—is compactly parameterized by a single dimensionless slope $D(T)\geq 0$ :

$$ \frac{\kappa_{xy}}{\kappa_{xy}^{(n)}}\simeq 1-D(T)\left(1-\frac{\lvert H\rvert}{H_{\mathrm{c}2}}\right). $$

As shown by the linear fits in Fig. 3(c), $D(T)$ increases on cooling, driving the extrapolated zero-field intercept $1-D(T)$ to reverse sign near $3.5\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$ before saturating at $2.1\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$ . While this intermediate-field intercept should not be conflated with the true zero-field Hall response, its sign reversal below $3.5\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$ is a direct signature of the smaller superconducting gap on the hole band: in a single-band superconductor, a linear mixed-state recovery of $\kappa_{xy}/H$ should simply vanish as $H,T\to 0$ without changing sign.

Microscopically, because electron and hole bands enter $\kappa_{xy}$ with opposite signs and scale as $\kappa_{xy,i}\propto HR_{i}\tau_{i}^{2}$ , the observed $H\lvert H\rvert$ term can arise from the field dependence of either the BQP population ( $R_{i}$ ) or the vortex-scattering relaxation time ( $\tau_{i}$ ). Notably, the simple substitution of a mean-field gap suppression $\Delta_{i}(H)\propto\sqrt{1-\lvert H\rvert/H_{\mathrm{c}2}}$ into the standard BRT integral yields $1-R_{i}\propto(1-\lvert H\rvert/H_{\mathrm{c}2})^{3/2}$ near $H_{\mathrm{c}2}$ , which has a vanishing slope at $H_{\mathrm{c}2}$ and fails to produce the linear behavior in Eq. (2). By contrast, the microscopic mixed-state treatment of Caroli and Cyrot [37] yields a leading-order correction proportional to the spatially averaged order parameter $\langle\lvert\Delta\rvert^{2}\rangle\propto 1-\lvert H\rvert/H_{\mathrm{c}2}$ , directly matching our experimental field dependence. Establishing how far below $H_{\mathrm{c}2}$ this linear regime extends in a multiband vortex lattice remains an important open question for theory.

Figure 3(e) summarizes our results in an $H$ – $T$ phase diagram of $\kappa_{xy}/\kappa_{xy}^{(n)}$ , overlaid with $H_{\mathrm{c}2}(T)$ and the magnetic irreversibility field $H^{*}(T)$ from Fig. S2. Constrained by two-gap specific heat and normal-state magnetotransport, our thermal Hall measurements establish that the larger superconducting gap in CeRu2 resides on the electron band, while BQP excitations across the smaller hole gap govern the low-field sign reversal at low temperatures. At intermediate fields, vortex-state transport gives way to a linear Caroli–Cyrot recovery of $\kappa_{xy}/\kappa_{xy}^{(n)}$ toward the normal state, where both longitudinal and transverse Lorenz ratios converge to $L_{0}$ above $H_{\mathrm{c}2}$ . More broadly, whereas thermodynamic probes and longitudinal heat transport are insensitive to carrier sign—and often obscured by dominant phonon backgrounds—our work unifies parameter-free longitudinal BRT channels with band-dependent thermal Hall angles to isolate signed quasiparticle currents. This approach presents a general blueprint for assigning carrier bands to superconducting gaps and disentangling multiband quasiparticle dynamics across compensated, flat-band, and heavy-fermion superconductors.

Note added.—During the completion of this manuscript, we became aware of a related preprint on the thermal Hall effect in elemental Nb [38], which similarly observes a low-field sign reversal of $\kappa_{xy}$ below $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ arising from two-gap pairing on electron- and hole-like bands. The two studies are highly complementary: whereas Nb is strongly uncompensated with gaps differing by nearly an order of magnitude extracted from longitudinal fits, CeRu2 is a compensated system where two gaps of comparable magnitude are fixed independently by specific heat, enabling our explicit two-band BRT decomposition of $\kappa_{xy}(T,H)$ across the mixed state.

## Supplemental Material

### S0.1 Synthesis

Single crystals of CeRu2 were grown by the Czochralski method in a tetra-arc furnace equipped with a water-cooled copper hearth under a high-purity argon atmosphere. A $3.7\text{\,}\mathrm{g}$ stoichiometric charge of elemental Ce and Ru ( $1{:}2$ molar ratio) was melted and flipped 11 times prior to growth to ensure compositional homogeneity. The single crystal boule was pulled at $4.2\text{\,}\mathrm{mm}\text{\,}{\mathrm{h}}^{-1}$ with a clockwise hearth rotation of $9.8\text{\,}\mathrm{r}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{m}$ and a counterclockwise seed rotation of $2.2\text{\,}\mathrm{r}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{m}$ .

Samples for magnetometry and transport were sectioned from the as-grown boule using a wire saw. Across crystals from the growth, the residual resistivity ratio $\mathrm{RRR}=\rho_{xx}($300\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$)/\rho_{0}$ —where $\rho_{0}$ is the low-temperature normal-state residual resistivity extrapolated to $0\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$ from above $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ —ranges from 5–8. Bulk magnetization and susceptibility measurements were first performed on a cylindrical disk ( $T_{\mathrm{c}}=$5.8\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$$ ) of diameter $2\text{\,}\mathrm{mm}$ and thickness $0.44\text{\,}\mathrm{mm}$ . To eliminate sample-to-sample variations between bulk and transport probes, this same disk was subsequently sectioned into a rectangular bar of dimensions $$2\text{\,}\mathrm{mm}$\times$1\text{\,}\mathrm{mm}$\times$0.15\text{\,}\mathrm{mm}$$ for electrical and thermal transport measurements.

### S0.2 Transport and magnetometry measurements

Bulk magnetization measurements were carried out in a Quantum Design Magnetic Property Measurement System (MPMS) operated in vibrating sample magnetometer (VSM) mode, while electrical and thermal transport measurements were performed in a Quantum Design Physical Property Measurement System (PPMS). Thermal conductivity and thermal Hall measurements were conducted using a home-built steady-state one-heater, three-thermometer probe. A longitudinal heat current $J_{Q}$ was generated via a resistive chip heater driven by a Stanford Research Systems CS580 voltage-controlled current source, and the resulting longitudinal ( $\Delta T_{x}$ ) and transverse ( $\Delta T_{y}$ ) temperature gradients were measured using calibrated Lakeshore Cernox 1050 resistance temperature detectors (RTDs). Each thermometer was excited with a $100\text{\,}\mathrm{nA}$ AC current at $133.77\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz}$ sourced by a Keithley 6221, and the differential voltages were read out using Zurich Instruments MFLI lock-in amplifiers.

To account for geometric contact misalignment, the measured longitudinal and transverse thermal (electrical) resistivities were field-symmetrized and antisymmetrized, respectively, using positive and negative magnetic field sweeps. The thermal (electrical) conductivity tensor components were then obtained by matrix inversion. To ensure a uniform vortex state and avoid flux-trapping history effects between field polarities, the sample was thermally cycled above $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ and zero-field cooled (ZFC) prior to acquiring each positive and negative field sweep. Similarly, fixed-field temperature sweeps were recorded under ZFC conditions by cooling the sample in zero field to base temperature before applying the target magnetic field and warming through $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ .

### S0.3 Compensated two-band magnetotransport

To determine the normal-state carrier density and band mobilities of CeRu2, we simultaneously fit the field-dependent magnetoresistance $\Delta\rho_{xx}/\rho_{xx}(0)$ and Hall resistivity $\rho_{xy}(H)$ across multiple temperatures from $10\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$ to $50\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$ [Fig. S1(a,b)]. Motivated by band-structure calculations and de Haas–van Alphen measurements establishing CeRu2 as a compensated metal [26, 31], we enforce exact carrier compensation ( $n_{e}=n_{h}=n_{\mathrm{tot}}/2$ ). Within the semiclassical two-band Drude model, the longitudinal and transverse electrical conductivities are given by

$$ \displaystyle\sigma_{xx}(B) \displaystyle=\frac{n_{\mathrm{tot}}e}{2}\left(\frac{\mu_{e}}{1+(\mu_{e}B)^{2}}+\frac{\mu_{h}}{1+(\mu_{h}B)^{2}}\right), \displaystyle\sigma_{xy}(B) \displaystyle=\frac{n_{\mathrm{tot}}eB}{2}\left(-\frac{\mu_{e}^{2}}{1+(\mu_{e}B)^{2}}+\frac{\mu_{h}^{2}}{1+(\mu_{h}B)^{2}}\right), $$

where $B=\mu_{0}H$ , $e$ is the elementary charge, and $\mu_{e}(T)$ and $\mu_{h}(T)$ are the electron and hole mobilities, respectively. Here we use the sign convention $\rho_{xy}(B)=\sigma_{xy}/(\sigma_{xx}^{2}+\sigma_{xy}^{2})$ and $\rho_{xx}(B)=\sigma_{xx}/(\sigma_{xx}^{2}+\sigma_{xy}^{2})$ , such that both $\sigma_{xy}$ and $\rho_{xy}$ are negative for electrons and positive for holes.

At $10\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$ , we obtain $n_{e}=n_{h}=$1.8\text{\times}{10}^{21}\text{\,}{\mathrm{cm}}^{-3}$$ ( $n_{\mathrm{tot}}=$3.6\text{\times}{10}^{21}\text{\,}{\mathrm{cm}}^{-3}$$ ) and mobilities $\mu_{e}=$254\text{\,}{\mathrm{cm}}^{2}\text{\,}{\mathrm{V}}^{-1}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1}$$ and $\mu_{h}=$170\text{\,}{\mathrm{cm}}^{2}\text{\,}{\mathrm{V}}^{-1}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1}$$ . Because $\mu_{e}>\mu_{h}$ , the electron band dominates the normal-state Hall response, accounting for the negative slope of $\rho_{xy}(H)$ in Fig. S1(b). Below $50\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$ , the mobility ratio remains nearly constant at

$$ r\equiv\frac{\mu_{h}}{\mu_{e}}\approx 0.68. $$

This mobility ratio directly constrains several normal-state and superconducting transport parameters:

#### 1. Zero-field electronic thermal conductivity weights.

In the low-temperature normal state ( $B\to 0$ ), where the Wiedemann–Franz law $\kappa_{xx,i}^{(n)}=L_{0}\sigma_{xx,i}^{(n)}T$ holds for each band, $i\in\{e,h\}$ , carrier compensation ( $n_{e}=n_{h}$ ) fixes the ratio of the hole- to electron-band normal-state thermal conductivities solely through the mobility ratio:

$$ \frac{\kappa_{xx,h}^{(n)}}{\kappa_{xx,e}^{(n)}}=\frac{n_{h}e\mu_{h}}{n_{e}e\mu_{e}}=\frac{\mu_{h}}{\mu_{e}}=r. $$

Consequently, one finds the fractional hole weight $c_{h}=\sigma_{xx,h}^{(n)}/(\sigma_{xx,e}^{(n)}+\sigma_{xx,h}^{(n)})$ in the zero-field BRT decomposition is fixed by

$$ c_{h}=\frac{r}{1+r}\approx 0.4,\qquad c_{e}=1-c_{h}\approx 0.60, $$

in remarkable agreement with the value obtained when leaving $c_{h}$ as an unconstrained fitting parameter in $\kappa_{xx}(T)$ below $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ .

#### 2. Effective mass and quasiparticle scattering time ratios.

Combining the magnetotransport mobility ratio with our specific heat analysis yields the relative effective masses and relaxation times of the two carrier types. Within a spherical Fermi-surface approximation, the volumetric Sommerfeld coefficient of band $i$ is $\gamma_{V,i}=(k_{\mathrm{B}}^{2}k_{F,i}/3\hbar^{2})m_{i}^{*}$ , where $k_{F,i}=(3\pi^{2}n_{i})^{1/3}$ . Because $n_{e}=n_{h}$ fixes $k_{F,e}=k_{F,h}$ , the ratio of the band effective masses is determined directly by the ratio of the Sommerfeld weights $a_{h}=$0.18\pm\pm 0.02$$ and $a_{e}=$0.83\pm\pm 0.02$$ from Table S1:

$$ \frac{m_{h}^{*}}{m_{e}^{*}}=\frac{a_{h}}{a_{e}}\approx 0.22. $$

This confirms that the electron sheets (which carry predominantly Ce $4f$ character near $\Gamma$ ) are nearly five times heavier than the hole sheets in an effective two-band model. Using $\mu_{i}=e\tau_{i}/m_{i}^{*}$ , the ratio of the quasiparticle transport relaxation times is

$$ \frac{\tau_{h}}{\tau_{e}}=\frac{\mu_{h}m_{h}^{*}}{\mu_{e}m_{e}^{*}}=r\frac{a_{h}}{a_{e}}\approx 0.14, $$

indicating that holes scatter approximately seven times more strongly than electrons in the normal state. Furthermore these transport parameters establish the microscopic length scales governing mixed-state transport. From the zero-temperature upper critical field $\mu_{0}H=$6.5\text{\,}\mathrm{T}$$ [Eq. (12)], the Ginzburg-Landau coherence length is $\xi_{0}=\sqrt{\Phi_{0}/[2\pi\mu_{0}H_{\mathrm{c}2}(0)]}\approx$7.1\text{\,}\mathrm{nm}$$ . Using the carrier density $n_{e}=n_{h}=$1.8\text{\times}{10}^{21}\text{\,}{\mathrm{cm}}^{-3}$$ ( $k_{F}\approx$3.8\text{\,}\mathrm{nm}$$ ) and the $10\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$ mobilities, the normal-state electronic mean free paths $\ell_{i}=\hbar k_{F}\mu_{i}/e$ are $\ell_{e}\approx$6.3\text{\,}\mathrm{nm}$$ and $\ell_{h}\approx$4.2\text{\,}\mathrm{nm}$$ . Both carrier sheets therefore operate in the moderately dirty limit ( $\ell_{i}\leq\xi_{0}$ ), consistent with the residual resistivity ratio $\mathrm{RRR}=\text{5--8}$ . This regime directly underpins two key aspects of our analysis: (i) elastic impurity scattering dominates over inelastic scattering below $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ , pinning the baseline relaxation times $\tau_{i}$ so that the low-field temperature dependence of $\kappa_{xy}$ in Eq. (1) is controlled by the zero-field BRT population factors $R_{i}(T)$ and (ii) the dirty-limit condition $\ell_{i}\leq\xi_{0}$ rigorously justifies applying the microscopic Caroli-Cyrot vortex-lattice expansion [37] to describe the linear-in- $H$ recovery of $\kappa_{xy}/\kappa_{xy}^{(n)}$ in Eq. (2).

#### 3. Consistency between $\sigma_{xx}$ , $R_{H}$ , and the thermal Hall prefactor $\lambda_{0}$ .

From the extracted $10\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$ parameters ( $n_{e}=$1.8\text{\times}{10}^{21}\text{\,}{\mathrm{cm}}^{-3}$$ , $\mu_{e}+\mu_{h}=$424\text{\,}{\mathrm{cm}}^{2}\text{\,}{\mathrm{V}}^{-1}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1}$$ ), the zero-field electrical conductivity is determined by $\sigma_{xx}(0)=n_{e}e(\mu_{e}+\mu_{h})\approx$1.2\text{\times}{10}^{7}\text{\,}\mathrm{S}\text{\,}{\mathrm{m}}^{-1}$$ , which via the Wiedemann–Franz law predicts a normal-state electronic thermal conductivity

$$ \kappa_{\mathrm{el}}/T=L_{0}\sigma_{xx}(0)\approx$0.3\text{\,}\mathrm{W}\text{\,}{\mathrm{K}}^{-2}\text{\,}{\mathrm{m}}^{-1}$, $$

in quantitative agreement with our measured normal-state $\kappa_{\mathrm{el}}/T$ .

Similarly, in the low-field limit, the normal-state thermal Hall angle of band $i$ is $\tan\theta_{i}=(L_{xy}/L_{0})\mu_{i}B$ , where the factor $L_{xy}/L_{0}\approx 0.7$ – $0.85$ [Fig. 1(c)] accounts for the modest suppression of the transverse Lorenz ratio relative to $L_{0}$ . Substituting $b_{i}(B)=(c_{i}\kappa_{\mathrm{el}}/\lambda_{0}T)\lvert\tan\theta_{i}\rvert$ into the normal-state boundary condition $b_{e}(B)-b_{h}(B)=B$ [with $c_{e}\mu_{e}-c_{h}\mu_{h}=(\mu_{e}^{2}-\mu_{h}^{2})/(\mu_{e}+\mu_{h})=\mu_{e}-\mu_{h}$ for a compensated metal] yields an explicit relation for the normal-state thermal Hall prefactor $\lambda_{0}=-\kappa_{xy}^{(n)}/(BT)$ :

$$ \lambda_{0}=\frac{L_{xy}}{L_{0}}\frac{\kappa_{\mathrm{el}}}{T}(\mu_{e}-\mu_{h}). $$

Evaluating Eq. (10) using our independently measured transport parameters— $\mu_{e}-\mu_{h}=$84\text{\,}{\mathrm{cm}}^{2}\text{\,}{\mathrm{V}}^{-1}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1}$$ , $\kappa_{\mathrm{el}}/T\approx$0.3\text{\,}\mathrm{W}\text{\,}{\mathrm{K}}^{-2}\text{\,}{\mathrm{m}}^{-1}$$ , and $L_{xy}/L_{0}\approx 0.7$ —predicts $\lambda_{0}\approx$1.7\text{\times}{10}^{-3}\text{\,}\mathrm{W}\text{\,}{\mathrm{K}}^{-2}\text{\,}{\mathrm{m}}^{-1}\text{\,}{\mathrm{T}}^{-1}$$ , in excellent agreement with the value $\lambda_{0}\approx$1.6\text{\times}{10}^{-3}\text{\,}\mathrm{W}\text{\,}{\mathrm{K}}^{-2}\text{\,}{\mathrm{m}}^{-1}\text{\,}{\mathrm{T}}^{-1}$$ measured directly from $\kappa_{xy}^{(n)}$ . Finally, we note that evaluating the Hall coefficient directly from Fig. S3 at $6\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$ yields $R_{H}\approx-$6\text{\times}{10}^{-10}\text{\,}{\mathrm{m}}^{3}\text{\,}{\mathrm{C}}^{-1}$$ ; while the thermal analog

$$ R_{H}=\frac{1}{n_{e}e}\frac{\mu_{h}-\mu_{e}}{\mu_{h}+\mu_{e}}=-\frac{\lambda_{0}}{\sigma_{xx}(0)}\left[\frac{L_{xy}}{L_{0}}\frac{\kappa_{\mathrm{el}}}{T}\right]^{-1}, $$

yields $R_{H}\approx-$5\text{\times}{10}^{-10}\text{\,}{\mathrm{m}}^{3}\text{\,}{\mathrm{C}}^{-1}$$ , within experimental agreement.

Isothermal magnetization curves $M(H)$ in the main panel of Fig. S2 allow us to track both the magnetic irreversibility field $H^{*}(T)$ (filled triangles) and the upper critical field $H_{\mathrm{c}2}(T)$ (open triangles). The field window between $H^{*}(T)$ and $H_{\mathrm{c}2}(T)$ widens substantially upon cooling, delineating the pinned vortex regime plotted in the phase diagram of Fig. 3(e) in the main text.

### S0.5 Specific heat analysis

Specific heat measurements were performed on a second single crystal with a nearly identical transition temperature $T_{\mathrm{c}}=$5.95\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$$ . In the normal state (measured at $$7\text{\,}\mathrm{T}$>\mu_{0}H_{\mathrm{c}2}$ ), the lattice contribution deviates from a simple $T^{3}$ power law below $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ due to phonon dispersion softening [32, 33]. We therefore model the normal-state specific heat above $H_{\mathrm{c}2}$ as

$$ C_{n}=\gamma_{n}T+\beta_{\mathrm{eff}}(T)T^{3}, $$

where $\gamma_{n}$ is the Sommerfeld coefficient and $\beta_{\mathrm{eff}}(T)=\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}/[1+(T/T_{s})^{2}]$ is an empirical parametrization of the temperature-dependent Debye coefficient. This corresponds to an effective Debye temperature $\Theta_{D}(T)=(12\pi^{4}N_{\mathrm{at}}R/5\beta_{\mathrm{eff}})^{1/3}$ , where $N_{\mathrm{at}}=3$ is the number of atoms per formula unit and $R=$8.3145\text{\,}\mathrm{J}\text{\,}{\mathrm{mol}}^{-1}\text{\,}{\mathrm{K}}^{-1}$$ is the ideal gas constant. In the zero-temperature limit, $\beta_{\mathrm{eff}}(0)=\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}$ yields a Debye temperature in good agreement with values independently derived from ultrasonic elastic constants [39].

To isolate the electronic specific heat in the zero-field superconducting state, $C_{\mathrm{es}}(T)=C(T)-\beta_{\mathrm{eff}}(T)T^{3}$ , we subtract the phonon background $\beta_{\mathrm{eff}}(T)T^{3}$ determined from the $7\text{\,}\mathrm{T}$ data. Within BCS theory, the electronic specific heat of a single isotropic gap $\Delta(T)$ is given by [25]

$$ \begin{split}C_{s}(T,\Delta)=\frac{3\gamma_{n}}{2\pi^{2}k_{\mathrm{B}}^{3}T^{2}}\int_{0}^{\infty}\left(E^{2}-\frac{T}{2}\frac{\differential\Delta^{2}}{\differential T}\right)\\
\times\frac{\differential\xi}{\cosh^{2}\!\left[E/(2k_{\mathrm{B}}T)\right]},\end{split} $$

where $E=\sqrt{\xi^{2}+\Delta^{2}(T)}$ is the Bogoliubov quasiparticle excitation energy. We approximate the temperature dependence of each gap using the standard BCS interpolation formula $\Delta_{i}(T)=\Delta_{i}\tanh\left(\eta\sqrt{T_{\mathrm{c}}/T-1}\right)$ with $\eta=1.74$ [40].

To account for multiband pairing across the electron and hole sheets within the well-known $\alpha$ -model type heat capacity, we express the total superconducting electronic specific heat as a weighted sum of two independent BCS channels plus a small residual linear contribution $\gamma_{\mathrm{res}}T$ :

$$ C_{\mathrm{es}}=a_{e}C_{s}(T,\Delta_{e}(T))+a_{h}C_{s}(T,\Delta_{h}(T))+\gamma_{\mathrm{res}}T, $$

where $a_{e}$ and $a_{h}$ represent the fractional contributions of the electron and hole bands to the normal-state Sommerfeld coefficient $\gamma_{n}$ (proportional to their respective partial densities of states at the Fermi level). The resulting best-fit parameters and uncertainties are summarized in Table S1. Crucially, even without enforcing a strict sum-rule constraint during optimization, the extracted weights satisfy $(a_{e}+a_{h})\gamma_{n}+\gamma_{\mathrm{res}}\approx\gamma_{n}$ , confirming entropy conservation and full thermodynamic consistency with the normal-state Sommerfeld coefficient extracted at $7\text{\,}\mathrm{T}$ .

### S0.6 BRT model in the mixed state

With the theory developed by Bardeen, Rickayzen, and Tewordt (BRT) [24], the suppression of the electronic thermal conductivity in an $s$ -wave superconductor relative to its normal-state value is governed by the universal function

$$ R(y)=\frac{2F_{1}(-y)+2y\ln(1+e^{-y})+y^{2}/(1+e^{y})}{2F_{1}(0)}, $$

where $y=\Delta(T,H)/(k_{\mathrm{B}}T)$ is the reduced gap and $F_{1}(-y)$ is the Fermi–Dirac integral

$$ F_{1}(-y)=\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{z\,\differential z}{1+e^{z+y}}=\frac{\pi^{2}}{12}-\int_{0}^{y}\ln(1+e^{-z})\,\differential z, $$

with $F_{1}(0)=\pi^{2}/12$ . Neglecting interband scattering between the electron and hole sheets, the total electronic thermal conductivity in the superconducting state is given by the weighted sum of the two bands:

$$ \frac{\kappa_{xx,e}(T)+\kappa_{xx,h}(T)}{\kappa_{\mathrm{el}}(T)}=(1-c_{h})R_{e}(T)+c_{h}R_{h}(T), $$

where $R_{i}(T)\equiv R\left(\Delta_{i}(T)/k_{\mathrm{B}}T\right)$ for $i\in\{e,h\}$ . In the zero-field analysis presented in the main text [Fig. 1(d)], the gap magnitudes $\Delta_{e,h}(T)$ are fixed by zero-field specific heat, the fractional hole weight $c_{h}$ is fixed by the normal-state mobility ratio $\mu_{h}/\mu_{e}$ , and the total normal-state electronic thermal conductivity $\kappa_{\mathrm{el}}(T)=L_{0}T\sigma_{xx}(T)$ is obtained from the electrical conductivity measured at $9\text{\,}\mathrm{T}$ via the Wiedemann–Franz law (Fig. S3). Notably, if $c_{h}$ is instead left as an unconstrained fitting parameter in Eq. (18), fitting the zero-field thermal conductivity independently converges to the same hole weight, confirming the self-consistency of our parameter-free decomposition.

The field dependence of $\kappa_{xx}(H)$ in the mixed state provides an independent test of this two-band electronic decomposition and rules out attributing the low-temperature thermal conductivity to an unphysically large phonon background. In the mixed state, phonon-vortex scattering reduces the lattice thermal conductivity according to $\kappa_{\mathrm{ph}}(H)=\kappa_{\mathrm{ph}}(0)/(1+zH)$ , where $z$ parametrizes the vortex-scattering cross section [23]. This expression serves as a strict upper bound on $\kappa_{\mathrm{ph}}(H)$ because, in addition to vortex core scattering, the field-induced recovery of the BQP population restores phonon-electron scattering toward its normal-state rate, further damping $\kappa_{\mathrm{ph}}(H)$ .

As shown in Fig. S4 at $T=$2.1\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$$ , attributing the electronic heat current solely to the larger gap ( $\tilde{c}_{h}=0$ , blue dotted curve) severely underestimates the recovery of $\kappa_{xx}(H)$ at intermediate fields because the phonon channel (green dashed curve) is rapidly quenched by vortex scattering. Conversely, a single small gap ( $\tilde{c}_{h}=1$ , red dotted curve) overestimates the low-field recovery. ### S0.7 Debye–Callaway model

To model the lattice thermal conductivity $\kappa_{\mathrm{ph}}(T)$ and its pronounced enhancement below $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ [Fig. 1(d) of the main text], we employ the Debye–Callaway model [41, 42, 43]. Assuming Matthiessen’s rule, the total phonon relaxation rate $\tau_{\mathrm{ph}}^{-1}$ is the sum of boundary ( $\tau_{\mathrm{bd}}^{-1}$ ), point-defect ( $\tau_{\mathrm{d}}^{-1}$ ), and phonon-electron ( $\tau_{\mathrm{ph-e}}^{-1}$ ) scattering rates:

$$ \tau_{\mathrm{ph}}^{-1}=\tau_{\mathrm{bd}}^{-1}+\tau_{\mathrm{d}}^{-1}+\tau_{\mathrm{ph-e}}^{-1}, $$

whose dependencies on the reduced phonon frequency $x=\hbar\omega/(k_{\mathrm{B}}T)$ and reduced temperature $t=T/T_{\mathrm{c}}$ are summarized in Table S2.

| Mechanism | Scattering rate |
|---|---|
| Boundary | $\tau_{\mathrm{bd}}^{-1}\propto\mathrm{const}$ |
| Point defect | $\tau_{\mathrm{d}}^{-1}\propto x^{4}t^{4}$ |
| Phonon-electron | $\tau_{\mathrm{ph-e}}^{-1}\propto xt\,g(x,y)$ |

*Table S2: Dominant phonon scattering mechanisms and their functional dependencies on the reduced phonon frequency $x=\hbar\omega/(k_{\mathrm{B}}T)$ , reduced gap $y=\bar{\Delta}/(k_{\mathrm{B}}T)$ , and reduced temperature $t=T/T_{\mathrm{c}}$ [44].*

Below $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ , the condensation of electronic states into the superconducting ground state suppresses phonon-electron scattering. According to BRT theory, the ratio of the superconducting- to normal-state phonon-electron scattering rates, $\tau_{\mathrm{ph-e,s}}^{-1}/\tau_{\mathrm{ph-e,n}}^{-1}=g(x,y)$ , is given by [24, 44]

$$ g(x,y)=\frac{1-e^{-x}}{x}\left[2J_{1}(x,y)+J_{2}(x,y)\right], $$

where $y=\bar{\Delta}(T)/(k_{\mathrm{B}}T)$ is the reduced gap, and the integrals $J_{1}(x,y)$ and $J_{2}(x,y)$ account for phonon scattering by thermally excited Bogoliubov quasiparticles and phonon-induced Cooper pair breaking/recombination (active only for phonon energies $\hbar\omega>2\bar{\Delta}$ , or $x>2y$ ), respectively. Above $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ , the vanishing of the gap ( $y=0$ ) yields $g(x,0)=1$ , smoothly recovering the normal-state metallic scattering rate. To avoid over-parametrizing the lattice fit with separate electron- and hole-band coupling constants, we evaluate $g(x,y)$ using a single density-of-states-weighted effective gap $\bar{\Delta}=a_{e}\Delta_{e}(T)+a_{h}\Delta_{h}(T)$ , where the gap magnitudes $\Delta_{e,h}(T)$ and Sommerfeld fractions $a_{e,h}$ are fixed directly by our specific heat analysis (Table S1). Factoring out the frequency- and temperature-independent boundary scattering rate $\tau_{\mathrm{bd}}^{-1}$ yields the dimensionless relative scattering rate

$$ r(x,t)\equiv\frac{\tau_{\mathrm{ph}}^{-1}}{\tau_{\mathrm{bd}}^{-1}}=1+\Gamma_{\mathrm{d}}x^{4}t^{4}+\Gamma_{\mathrm{ph\text{-}e}}xt\,g(x,y), $$

where $\Gamma_{\mathrm{d}}$ and $\Gamma_{\mathrm{ph\text{-}e}}$ parametrize the relative strengths of point-defect and phonon-electron scattering relative to boundary scattering. Within the Debye–Callaway model, the phonon thermal conductivity is then given by

$$ \kappa_{\mathrm{ph}}(T)=\Lambda t^{3}\int_{0}^{\Theta_{D}(T)/T}\frac{x^{4}e^{x}}{(e^{x}-1)^{2}}\frac{\differential x}{r(x,t)}, $$

where $\Lambda=(4\pi/3)^{1/3}k_{\mathrm{B}}^{2}T_{\mathrm{c}}^{3}\ell_{b}/[2\pi\hbar a^{2}\Theta_{D}^{2}(T)]$ , $a=$7.53\text{\,}\mathrm{\textup{\AA}}$$ is the conventional cubic lattice constant of CeRu2, and $\ell_{b}$ is the effective phonon boundary mean free path [44].

Because the electronic channels $\kappa_{xx,e}(T)$ and $\kappa_{xx,h}(T)$ are completely fixed by specific heat and normal-state magnetotransport, we fit $\kappa_{\mathrm{ph}}(T)$ directly to the residual lattice conductivity $\kappa_{xx}(T)-[\kappa_{xx,e}(T)+\kappa_{xx,h}(T)]$ . The fit yields a boundary mean free path $\ell_{b}=$0.9\pm\pm 0.1\text{\,}\mathrm{mm}$$ , comparable to the physical cross-sectional dimensions of the crystal. We find that phonon-electron scattering strongly dominates the thermal resistance near $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ ( $\Gamma_{\mathrm{ph\text{-}e}}=200\pm 20$ ), whereas point-defect scattering remains small, $\Gamma_{\mathrm{d}}(T)=1.7[\Theta_{D}(0)/\Theta_{D}(T)]^{4}$ (varying between $0.3<\Gamma_{\mathrm{d}}<1.7$ due to the temperature-dependent Debye temperature $\Theta_{D}(T)$ extracted from specific heat).
